summary: Defines how IP and ARP packets are transmitted over a Switched Multi-megabit Data Service network configured as a logical IP subnetwork. It is an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: This explains how to send Internet messages across a particular fast public data network.

questions: how is ip sent over smds
what is the mtu for ip over smds
how does arp work over smds
subtitle: How to carry IP and ARP over SMDS, a connectionless public data service, when it is set up as a logical IP subnetwork.

tldr.problem: SMDS is a public, connectionless packet-switched data service with its own addressing, so IP hosts needed an agreed way to send datagrams and resolve addresses over it.
tldr.mechanism: IP and ARP packets are wrapped in IEEE 802.2 LLC and SNAP headers inside SMDS frames, ARP maps IP addresses to SMDS addresses using a group address, and the IP MTU is 9180 octets.
tldr.outcome: The memo covers the logical IP subnetwork case only. It leaves broader public configurations to future documents and says security issues are not discussed.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1209 as an Internet Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFCs. The memo itself says it covers only logical IP subnetwork configurations and that other configurations would be treated in future documents.

sections.title: Introduction to SMDS
sections.content:
The goal is to allow compatible and interoperable implementations for transmitting IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies. The SMDS Service is a connectionless, public, packet-switched data service whose features resemble high-speed LANs.

  • Each data unit is switched separately, with no connection set up first.
  • It carries up to 9188 octets of user information in a single transmission.
  • There is no explicit flow control; an access class mechanism limits the transfer rate on access paths.
  • Individual and group-addressed (multicast) packets can be sent.
  • Source address validation and address screening let subscribers form a closed user group.

SMDS addresses are 60 bits plus a 4 bit Address Type. The value 1100 marks an individual address and 1110 a 60-bit group address.
sections.eli5: SMDS is like a public mail system for computers. Each message travels on its own, and each address has a little tag saying whether it names one computer or a whole group.

sections.title: Protocol Stack and Logical IP Subnetworks
sections.content:
The SMDS Interface Protocol (SIP) is based on the IEEE 802.6 Distributed Queue Dual Bus (DQDB) connectionless MAC protocol. The SMDS service layer corresponds to the IEEE 802 MAC sublayer, and the rest of the data link service comes from IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC).

The memo describes a logical IP subnetwork (LIS) configuration. Each administrative entity configures its hosts in a closed LIS that operates independently of other LISs on the same SMDS network. Hosts in a LIS talk directly. Reaching hosts outside it goes through an IP router that is a member of both subnetworks.

Requirements for a LIS: all members share the same IP network or subnet number, stations inside are reached directly over SMDS, stations outside are reached via a router, and one SMDS group address identifies all LIS members. The memo considers only directly connected stations and routers, not MAC level bridging.
sections.eli5: A LIS is like a private club on a public network. Members talk directly, and to reach anyone outside the club they ask a doorman, the router.

sections.title: Required Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
Each IP station MUST be configurable with three values, fixed at SMDS subscription time and different for each LIS:

  • smds$ha: the station's SMDS individual address, which it MUST accept datagrams for.
  • smds$lis-ga: the LIS group address, which all members MUST accept datagrams for.
  • smds$arp-req: the address where ARP requests are sent. In the initial LIS configuration it is set to smds$lis-ga.

Routers that interconnect LISs MUST support one set of these parameters per connected LIS, tied to an IP network or subnet number. The network side must configure the group address, and SMDS address screening tables are not needed for IP over SMDS. If they are used, they MUST allow direct communication among LIS hosts and use of the group address.
sections.eli5: Each computer needs to know its own mailbox number, the number for mail to the whole club, and where to ask questions about who is who.

sections.title: Packet Format and Size
sections.content:
IP and ARP packets are encapsulated in IEEE 802.2 LLC with an IEEE 802.1A SNAP header, carried in the 3-level SIP. Only LLC Type One Unnumbered Information is used. Multi-byte fields are big-endian.

  • The HLPI value in the SIP L3 header is 1.
  • The LLC and SNAP headers together are 8 octets.
  • DSAP and SSAP are 170 (decimal), AA hexadecimal, and Ctrl is 3.
  • The SNAP Org Code is zero.
  • The EtherType is 2048 (0800 hexadecimal) for IP and 2054 (0806 hexadecimal) for ARP.

SMDS allows 9188 information octets, which leaves 9180 after the LLC/SNAP header. The IP MTU SHALL therefore be 9180 octets. There is no minimum packet size. Trailer encapsulation, used by some 4.x BSD Unix versions, SHALL NOT be used.
sections.eli5: Each Internet message goes into an envelope with a few standard labels saying what kind of message it is. The biggest message that fits is 9180 octets.

sections.title: Address Resolution with ARP
sections.content:
Mapping 32-bit Internet addresses to SMDS addresses SHALL use ARP. Hosts MUST know their own Internet and SMDS addresses, answer ARP requests, and use ARP to find other hosts' SMDS addresses.

The ARP fields for SMDS are: hardware type 14 (0E hexadecimal), protocol type 2048 (0800 hexadecimal) for IP, hardware address length 8, protocol address length 4, and operation code 1 for request and 2 for reply. SMDS hardware addresses in ARP packets MUST be in native SMDS format.

Instead of a broadcast, an ARP request is sent to smds$arp-req, which in a LIS is the group address smds$lis-ga. The memo says that in a larger public configuration this might point at ARP server(s) instead.
sections.eli5: To find who owns an Internet address, a computer shouts the question to the whole club's group mailbox, and the owner answers.

sections.title: Broadcast, Multicast and 802.2 Details
sections.content:
SMDS has no complete hardware broadcast, so the IP broadcast address (host part all binary ones) MUST be mapped to smds$lis-ga.

For multicast, RFC 1112 needs dynamic join and leave operations that SMDS group addresses do not support. The memo therefore RECOMMENDS the method used for pure broadcast media: all multicast IP addresses map to the same address as broadcast, smds$lis-ga, and destination hosts MUST filter multicast packets.

All implementations MUST support IEEE 802.2 Class I service to be compliant, even parts not needed for IP and ARP, such as answering XID and TEST commands. The IP datagram's byte order maps directly onto the native SMDS byte order.
sections.eli5: Since there is no way to shout to everyone, the club's group mailbox is used for both shouts and group messages, and each computer ignores the ones it does not care about.
